prompt.context: The client is a Private Equity investor who has recently purchased a plastic pellet manufacturing company based in South Carolina. Plastic pellet manufacturing is the process of procuring waste or recycled plastics and transforming them into a pellet form so that it can be sold to companies needing to reproduce other plastic products. They sell these pellets exclusively to companies who produce plastic products. Current EBITDA is $100M.
prompt.question: She has approached our firm searching for several alternative strategies to improve EBITDA and firm value so that she can sell the firm for a profit within five years. What recommendations would you make?

clarifying_info.q: What does plastic pellet manufacturing involve?
clarifying_info.a: It is the process of procuring waste or recycled plastics and transforming them into pellet form to be sold to companies that produce other plastic products.
They sell exclusively to companies who produce plastic products.

clarifying_info.q: What is the target return or value improvement?
clarifying_info.a: She wants to improve the value of the firm by at least 3x.

exhibits.title: Supplier Pricing and Capacity
exhibits.shows: A table listing four suppliers (A, B, C, D) with their capacity in tons, price per 100 tons, price per 500 tons (where applicable), and unit transport cost per ton.

data.note: No other unit costs differ across suppliers

framework: Profit tree isolating pricing, volume, product mix, and fixed/variable costs
Analysis of strengths and weaknesses of the pellet company
Review of customer base and opportunities to expand
Potential additional revenue streams (e.g., specialized products)
(Exceptional) Opportunities to create synergies within the PE firm's portfolio

questions.prompt: What product mix issues exist, and how should the company address them?
questions.guidance: The company produces two types of pellets: Product A (post-consumer plastic, can only be used for new consumer products) and Product B (manufacturing scrap, can be made into anything). Product B has a higher margin than Product A. The company currently makes more of Product A because it has an excess inventory of raw material for Product A. The company runs at full capacity and can sell everything it produces. A strong candidate recognizes: (1) shifting production toward the higher-margin Product B would improve EBITDA without adding capacity; (2) the excess inventory for Product A is a constraint that could be resolved by selling it to a competitor, freeing up capacity to produce more Product B.

questions.prompt: What operational levers can improve EBITDA given that the plant is running at full capacity and labor/material costs cannot be cut?
questions.guidance: Because the market is commoditized and unionized, labor and material costs cannot be reduced. Market growth is flat and national demand is already being filled. Capacity is maxed out. Good responses focus on operational efficiency within the existing footprint: reducing lead times, improving turnaround time, optimizing inventory management, increasing throughput, reducing maintenance costs, and minimizing downtime. Candidates should note that any changes must pay off within the 5-year horizon, and adding new capacity is unlikely to be realistic in that timeframe.

questions.prompt: Create the optimal sourcing plan to procure 1,000 tons of plastic from the available suppliers.
questions.guidance: Calculate total unit cost (material price + transport cost) for each supplier at each available order quantity, then procure from cheapest sources first, respecting capacity constraints.

math.setup: Total unit cost = price per ton at given quantity + unit transport cost. Compare unit costs across suppliers and order quantities to minimize total procurement cost for 1,000 tons. Supplier capacities: A=1000t, B=500t, C=200t, D=100t.
steps: Calculate unit cost at 500 tons: A=2.50+0.25=2.75, B=2.35+0.50=2.85, C=N/A, D=N/A
Rank by unit cost: C@100t=2.50 (cheapest, max 200t), A@500t=2.75 (next cheapest, requires buying 500t), B@100t=2.90 (next, use for remainder)
Optimal plan: Buy all 200t from C (2.50/t), buy 500t from A at the 500-ton price tier (2.75/t), buy remaining 300t from B at the 100-ton price tier (2.90/t)
math.answer: Sourcing plan: A=500 tons, B=300 tons, C=200 tons. Total procurement cost = $2,745K (bonus calculation).

recommendation: Switch product mix to focus on the higher-margin Product B
Sell excess raw material inventory for Product A to competitors to free up production capacity
Review plant operations for cost-cutting opportunities (lead times, throughput, downtime, maintenance)

Develop a transition plan to shift production mix toward Product B
